utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's a filing from the Defence which I think Mr. Groome better be in court, perhaps at the end of this witness's evidence, so we can deal with it, about the expert witnesses. Right. Well, you proceed, Mr. Ossogo, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, yesterday we reached a certain point in your testimony, and we're going to go back to the area, geographical area in which you were operating, where you were before the corpses started floating down the Drina, which you noticed first, and then also where were the places where you buried the various bodies that you retrieved from the river in the area of Zepa and more specifically, in the surroundings of Slap. We have an aerial photograph here on which you will be able to show Their Honours these different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Try and get it between the English and the B/C/S booth so that at least somebody from there can see out, would you. Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it's best if you take the other microphone. No, the standing one. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you left your village to go to the Zepa region, and more specifically to Slap, but before starting to retrieve the bodies from the Drina River, you helped persons cross from one bank of the Drina River to the other. Could you show us where you were at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I crossed from this river bank to this river bank. These small houses that you see here, there were some camps here, and we crossed here for a while in these camps and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, sir. Let's wait until the usher is out of the way because he's right in our way and we can't see a thing. All right. Now that he's moved that, thank you, you proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We crossed from this side to the other. There was a camp here next to this small bridge. There's a hanging bridge here. This is a small river. It's called the Zepa, which flows into the Drina here. And there were some camps here, and we kept guard duty for about a month here, roughly along this route, next to this house, this way. These were our positions here. I lived -- I can't show you exactly. Slap is over here. It's about half a kilometre away along this road, and that is where I lived, where I was accommodated. And we pulled out the bodies from the Drina. This is the Drina. Through this pass under the bridge, and we carried them upstream, upstream along the Zepa River, and we pulled them out onto the bank here somewhere. About 1 kilometre upstream from the bridge, roughly here at this location. So roughly here somewhere. And that is where about 170 to 180 bodies are buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, what is the number, the Prosecution number on that aerial photograph labelled Slap?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It's 138 -- sorry, 139, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 139-1. We've just been handed it. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So could you please indicate which is the Drina River and which is the Zepa River more precisely. Where is the Zepa River, please?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina is here. This is the Drina, and this is the Zepa, and the Zepa flows into the Drina here, from this little bridge, 50 metres after the bridge, the Zepa flows into the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And the bodies that you retrieved from the river?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that there were two bridges on this river. So I don't know what the scale is. One was a hanging bridge, about 50 metres from the Drina, and there was another one about two kilometres upstream. It was like a monument bridge with an arch. No. I just remembered now. So this is exactly the bridge down there which is 50 metres from the Drina itself, and this is the river. And the location is here where we retrieved the bodies and buried them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's now a little muddled as far as I can see. I thought the witness said they actually retrieved them from the Drina and then took them under the bridge and then up to where he now says that he buried them. You better just get that clear from something he said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite correct, Mr. President. That brings me to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: From what direction were the bodies coming that you were retrieving. Before you pulled them out and took them up the Zepa River, where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Visegrad is here and I suppose it is, then the bodies were around the bend from the Drina River and we could see them at a distance of 1 kilometre. And usually using boats with oars, the boats were here or here in this small river, and we would row these boats up to this point and the bodies would be coming from that direction, and we would catch them here, four or five bodies per boat, with wooden hooks that were nailed to the boat. And those we couldn't catch, they went on down the river. They were pulled out here, and driven by boat. We would row those boats right up to this burial place where the bodies were buried. They were pulled out here to the shore, and this is where we carried out the -- whatever you would call it, this triage or the identification. We tried to see whether they had any identification papers for us to be able to identify them. That is what we did. So each body was picked up here, driven by boat up this river, and I would sit here on an old broken boat. There was a team working here searching the bodies, taking off clothes and other documents, and I would write down, "He was killed in such-and-such a way. He was wearing such-and-such clothes, we found such-and-such documents on him, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Poljo. And when the bodies could not be retrieved for the reasons you gave yesterday, the advanced stage of decomposition of the bodies, in what direction did those bodies move? You showed us what direction they came from, but when you were unable to pull them out, did they continue in the same direction? Would you show the Chamber the direction along which they flowed?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would let them flow down the river towards Paocici, Bajina Basta. They went downstream along the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So you're showing the down Stream direction of the river, are you?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not certain I'm reading the map properly, but I think that is so. I'm quite sure that this is that river and that these are those locations. I hope I'm not confused. Maybe Visegrad is down here. But I think it was as I told you, that the bodies were coming from this direction. We would catch five or six. Those we couldn't catch went on flowing down the river -- floating down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you need the photograph any more?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you need the photograph any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly if further clarification are required towards the examination-in-chief or during the cross-examination by the Defence, but for the moment, we don't need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, take it down so that the interpreters can see, would you. Thank you. Mr. Ossogo, on the other very large photograph that we've been shown, we were shown the flow of the river, but it obviously did not include the area of Slap. Is there a map either in evidence or to be tendered which shows us the whole of the general terrain so the witness can orient himself properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the only aerial photograph that we have, Mr. President. We had some problems with the witness during the proofing. He forgot his glasses, and we had a map with all the names for him to be able to complete this description that he gave on the basis of this photograph. Unfortunately, he forgot his glasses in Bosnia. So this was a risk, as I've said, in showing him this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But if you do have some map, surely somewhere in the huge organisation upstairs there's a magnifying glass that will help the witness to read the names on the map. It's just that if there is any problem about this, I don't see one, perhaps we could wait until the cross-examination, but if there is any problem, we want to make absolutely certain that he has his bearings right in relation to that photograph. Let's see what Mr. Domazet does in cross-examination, and if it's necessary, we'll give you an adjournment to enable the witness to have a look at the map with a magnifying glass. Now, you proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There is a map available, and if necessary, Mr. Poljo can use it, looking at it from a distance, and maybe if he moves it away sufficiently, he will be able to read it, and we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There comes a time, I'm afraid, when your arms are not long enough to correct your deficiencies in visual acuity. Are you going to tender this photograph that has been used? Is there any objection to that, Mr. Domazet? That's the document marked 139-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. No, Your Honour. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be Exhibit P139.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, we stopped yesterday at the point when you were indicating the condition of the bodies that you were pulling out of the Drina River, and I was just asking you the type of clothing that could be found on these bodies. Were they civilian clothes, military uniforms, or any other type of clothing?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as military dress is concerned, no military uniforms. There weren't bodies wearing military uniforms. But police uniforms were encountered. I remember one or two bodies clothed in police uniforms. Long coats, I think they were wearing. Something like that. The rest were wearing civilian clothes. Maybe I forgot your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question. That was the answer. Did you hear any reference to some bodies identified by you during this operation, did you hear their names mentioned during subsequent exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean really. Could you explain what exactly you mean? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you asked to participate in the exhumations in order to identify those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? In what time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After you completed the operation that you have described to us in Slap.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe a year ago -- I think it was more than a year ago that representatives of the International Community, the police, and some security forces, anyway, they were in jeeps, came to pick me up, and they picked up another guy who lived in this village of Slap, and they asked us if we could remember to show them this grave. And we showed them the location, and these gentlemen took some photographs. I think that two graves or two numbers were dug up, and they were able to see for themselves that there were corpses in those graves. They covered them up again and they left, and I know nothing more about it. I just know that later on, there was another exhumation, that they exhumed some bodies and that they transferred them to Visoko a couple of months ago. I don't remember exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poljo, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poljo, you said in your testimony regarding the first case, the first body that was noticed around mid-May, which you pulled out of the river, you said that the examination was carried out by the police from Rogatica and the judicial bodies and that you were present. Do you know anything more about the result of their investigation? Did they establish who the person was and how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That first body which came down the Drina, I personally, together with two others, two other locals, we were going hunting for game, and we were going from Slap down the Drina for a couple of kilometres and we noticed this body floating on the river, and we hooked the body to our boat and took it back to Slap. And we called up by telephone from Zepa the police. We called the police in Rogatica to come to carry out the inquest. Some forensic experts arrived, and they carried out the inspection. There was no document on this man. It was a man in his 60s. He had pills on him, as if he was suffering there diabetes. He was a diabetic patient. And they took the report with them to Rogatica, and for 10 or 15 days there was no communication with Rogatica, the lines were down, the telephone was down, except for a single radio station that remained in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, this judicial team of experts did not inform you of any details.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me anything. They packed their bags, got into the car, and left for Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that, when the subsequent bodies were pulled out of the river, did you try again to call these people from Rogatica or not to carry out the examination?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on it was not possible to contact Rogatica because there was no electricity, the telephone lines were down, combat operations started, and people were fleeing Rogatica; that is, the Muslim population fled to Zepa. The lines, the front lines, were already formed around Zepa, and the defence of Zepa, the defence lines around Zepa had already been formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, you said today that you were able to see the bodies roughly a kilometre away from the spot where you stood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We would usually see the bodies from the houses in Slap. This may be even more than a kilometre away if we were looking from where the camps were where we kept guard duty. So we watched the time. It took the body about one hour to float to where we were. Nobody measured this distance, but that is an indication for you. They would reach us an hour later. The Drina was not a very fast-flowing river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question and that is why I asked you about the distance. So it took about one hour from the moment the body was spotted for it to reach you and to be pulled out. I see.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigator, you said that during the first week, you didn't pull out bodies and that ten or so bodies floated by without you pulling them out, and that after that first week you started retrieving the bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More than ten bodies went by. Bodies were passing in daytime and night-time. We couldn't see them during the night, and I am saying what we saw during the daytime. And I'm sure that more bodies went by. And if you're interested in a figure, I think between 500 and 600 bodies floated down the river, because once when the rain was pouring heavily and the river was high, we saw 20 to 30 bodies, and there was one guy who managed to pull out four or five because he was brave, and all the rest went by. There was livestock floating down. There was some furniture, TV sets. Probably those bodies had been thrown into a smaller river and when the water level rose, the tributaries -- the bodies from the tributaries appeared in the Drina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was just going to ask that, because yesterday you said that according to your estimate, you pulled out only 20 per cent of the corpses from the Drina. So I was going to ask how come you managed to retrieve only such a small percentage if you were on duty constantly on the Drina banks. So is this the explanation?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I never tried to calculate the percentage. I was on guard one night, and I would pull out a body or two with the boat. It was a terrible job. And I did so mostly because I had two brothers and an uncle working up there in various companies, but I'm quite sure that many more floated by. Between 500 and 600. I'm quite sure to this day there are bodies there. Those bodies got caught in the branches, among the stones, and when the water level rose, some of these bodies got unhooked and started floating again. The stench was so terrible that you really couldn't stand it, and we didn't touch those who were totally decomposed. We let them float by. This is really not something to joke about, but there was a body that we pulled out among a group of four or five, and when we started the search, there were no documents on him. Then these four or five men were working on this, and when they took off his trousers, he had a jogging suit underneath, and on this body they found some money, new -- a couple of new banknotes with the words "Branch office Banja Luka" on them. And in his other pocket -- his pockets were chequerboard, like the Croatian flag, and in one pocket there was a piece of -- double piece of paper with poems written on them. The man may have been a poet, or when he had a drink too many he was forced to sing. And the poem was about Alija, "Alija with a red fez, you will eat pork meat and you will disappear with the seed of Muslims. Korturinci [phoen] are the best guys. They're not afraid of knives because they have seven centimetre thick skin." Then one of us said, "Look, he could be a Serb," because he wasn't circumcised. And then they said, "Throw him into the Drina. He's a Serb." And we kept him under the water for a day and night. Then there were all kind of suggestions that he should be sent to Bajina Basta. We hooked him to a tree, and we thought maybe we could exchange him if he was a Serb or Croat. And somebody unhooked him the next day or the water unhooked him and he went down the river. This was a bit funny, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I understood, you kept guard duty on the Drina banks round the clock, not because of the bodies but because you were on guard duty and this applied to you and the other people with you?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I crossed the Drina River, when Sabanovic released the water from the dam, I was at home watching television and I saw the water being released - I don't know how many days later it was that I crossed the river, and for a month later there were no other bodies and I was on guard duty. And when we saw the bodies, I made the suggestion and asked the others to join, that if we can't help our own people, our neighbours in any other way, then we should at least try to bury them properly so they would know where their graves are. Afterwards, I was released from guard duty, and I worked on this -- I don't know whether you call it exhumation, but I took down the notes. One team was pulling out the bodies, another was searching them, and I was taking down the notes, and that was my work duty all summer. I was away for a few days. I went to Krusev Dol looking for food, but otherwise I was there. That was the period I was absent for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer is broader than my question. My question was whether you were on guard duty day and night, and you said yes. You said or you're telling me now that you tried to pull out bodies during the night as well.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would happen at night-time, too, but we did most of the retrieval in the morning and in the evening because there was shelling. A couple of times this man, who pulled out 50 per cent of the bodies, and he was exposed to shelling during the daytime. Sometimes at night, too, if the guards noticed anything, and in the morning when it was still misty we did most of the retrieval.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you -- yesterday when you spoke about somebody's dead came in sheets or blankets, and in answer to the question of the Prosecution whether this was from an institution or a hotel, you said that there was talk about this, and in the discussion it was said that it was possible that they were from there, but you weren't sure about it. As far as I could understand, you had no material evidence about the origin of those blankets, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for the first body, the female body wrapped up in a blanket, well, I think that I saw some of these blankets in the room of Amir Suceska, that he had similar blankets in his room. About the others, well, I was not quite sure, because we didn't really look. It was necessary to remove the female person as quickly as possible so as not to be seen by her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, all these bodies that went down the Drina, where did they originate from? Where could they have come from?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of Visegrad. That is where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it possible that they could have come from Foca?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a dam there in Visegrad. Well, what we could see, and I know Visegrad quite well, that many bodies came from my place. I worked there for quite some time, and I know many of the inhabitants personally. There were people from Zupa. Fifty per cent of men and women from Zepa were there, and when the bodies would be coming, they'd come and try to identify members of their family if there were no documents there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, as far as I can understand, you had identified some of the bodies, that you recognised some of them, and that you recognised them as people from Visegrad and the area. But my question was: Was it possible -- can you exclude the possibility that some of these bodies had come from Foca or Gorazde and the surrounding settlements? Can you rule out that possibility or not?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember a body. There was a soldier who was from the JNA. He had done his military service, and he stayed longer -- he prolonged -- he stayed there for four months, and there we have some kind of document on him. I forgot his name. And he came as far as Visegrad by bus. He had a ticket. And in that paper, it said that he was released and also members of his family actually were free from any form of mobilisation. This young man was wearing civilian clothes. I think it was jeans he was wearing, slacks, and a jeans jacket, as far as I remember, and that he was from Rogatica. That he was from Rogatica, I can remember that. I cannot remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poljo. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, you have -- you stated yesterday that there were two bodies --

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I shall recommence. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: See what you can do.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have some other earphones, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Give the witness the original ones he was using.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you hear it? Can you hear now, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Mevsud, in your statement of yesterday, you said that there were two bodies of young women coming from Lasci, a place not far from the Hotel Vilina Vlas, and the bodies of these women were wrapped up in sheets and could have belonged -- these sheets could have belonged to that hotel. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but I'm not sure about the others, about the two women from that hotel. This is hearsay, actually, because the blankets were different from those that I had seen first. The colour wasn't the same, and some said that the women that had come, that they had come from a place above the Hotel Vilina Vlas and they had to pass through there. And on the basis of that story, I concluded that they could have been those. And one of them was wearing clothes from that village. Then I would have thought that these persons, that they could have been, in fact, detained in Vilina Vlas Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Well, you indicate -- you had stated that there were sheets and not blankets. There is a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for me, blankets are the same as sheets. Well, perhaps you thought of bed linen. Is that what you had in mind? I don't know what exactly you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. In the translation we had, the word "blankets" was mentioned, but in fact, what were they wrapped up in, the bodies, in sheets or blankets? Blankets are heavy and sheets are light.

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In blankets, in two blankets. They were rolled up in them, and this was tied up with wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Poljo, you said you were keeping some notes about -- you were describing those bodies from the river. Can you tell me what happened with those notebooks or notes and other objects which were collected on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that notebook remained in Slap, in the home -- buried in the yard in the house where I was living, in the house of Jusuf Begovic, Ibrahim Begovic. It was a pail. I think It was a tin pail. Perhaps oil had been in it before. About 25 litres could fit in. In that pail, when these documents were dried during the day, we put that -- those documents inside. The pail was in the cellar. When the military operations took place in Zepa, I was on guard, and a messenger came and told me that we could not defend Zepa, that the Serb forces were coming in from the direction of Rogatica and the whole population had to be evacuated in the direction of Srebrenica. I came back home at 12.30 at night. My wife wrote a note to me and said that she had gone near -- in the direction of Sarina Bukva. It was a mountain in the direction of Srebrenica. Well, I took a jacket then, and I took my rifle, and found them near Krusev Dol. And people were there at 1.00 in the morning. Most people had left Zepa and they went to Srebrenica and Krusev Dol, in the mountains where the positions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: Do you know where the notebooks are now? Have you seen them since you put them in the pail in Slap?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left and I spent three days in the mountains. In Zepa, no one was there, neither the Serb forces nor our forces. There was no one in Zepa at the time. And in the mountains, we were debating whether to go back, who should go back or not go back. We who were refugees, we did not want to go back to Zepa. We wanted to go to Tuzla and Srebrenica. The bravest indeed went back during the night, took food in Zepa and brought it to the mountains again. Ibrahim, my boss, he went back, and some other young persons from my area and stayed there, but I did not want to go back with my family, with my brother's family, my parents. My father and brother went there. They took the cow in the direction of the forest, in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you again. Now, look, please. This question may be answered yes or no and then you may be asked another one. Have you seen those notes since you put them in the pail?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw them again because I didn't go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you heard what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MEVSUD POLJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Yes, I did hear what happened to them. This gentleman told me, whose house I lived in, who went back. And my father, my father's name was Ibro, and was the house of Ibrahim. And when this messenger came telling them they had to leave the village, they took the bucket from the cellar, and they dug it next to a walnut tree. That is what my father told me. And later on, when he moved to Kakanj, he died afterwards, they told me where they had buried this bucket. And the people from International Community, when they came, they asked me whether I could indicate the place, and we went there. We tried to find it in two different places. It was very hot. We didn't have the proper digging machinery. It was overgrown, the area, so I was unable to indicate the exact spot for us to be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I understood that information couldn't be used in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, do you want to ask any questions arising out of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How about you, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Just a moment ago you referred to a map which might complement the information obtained from Exhibit 139.1. We have a map here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ossogo, there's no cross-examination about that so there's no challenge to his evidence. So there's no need to worry about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Thank you. No questions for our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming to give evidence and for the evidence which you gave. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may ask it. I don't know whether we will be able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are here from the whole world to provide questions nicely and fairly for everyone. What I would like to know, it appears here that only Vasiljevic is on trial. Do you know that in the municipality of Visegrad there were both Serbs and Muslims killed, numbering 2.500 to 3.000? So is it only this one man whom you have arrested and brought here or something else is at stake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We do know something of the numbers who were killed and it is matter of great importance. There are other people charged. The problem is this Tribunal has no power to go out and arrest them. It relies upon SFOR and similar agencies to make the arrests; for example, the authorities of Republika Srpska. Republika Srpska has never arrested anybody for us, and SFOR has varying bursts of enthusiasm. But you can be assured that there are other people who have been charged. How many, I don't know. Mr. Vasiljevic is on trial in this case alone simply because we do not have the other people arrested and in our custody, and we are attempting, as I understand it, to follow up on two other persons who have been seen in the municipality of Visegrad. But we understand your concern, sir, and that is one of the problems with the way in which the United Nations has set up this Tribunal. Unfortunately, we are unable to change that. I hope that explains your concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If that is just one man, he couldn't have killed or massacred so many chicks. I'm not referring to Vasiljevic in person, but for a single person it would take two years to kill that many people, to beat up and mutilate people. So it's not just a question of killing with firearms. There were people who were beaten and tortured for days. I could beat up two men today and the next day I couldn't beat anyone. So every other person was beaten up, which means there are a large number of people who are responsible. I never dreamt in 1992 that I would be coming here. I feel a bit awkward, embarrassed because of Vasiljevic himself. We know each other. We would sit together and have a drink together. His wife worked with me. We were colleagues from work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, sir. We understand that. You have given evidence in this case about matters other than those which concern Mr. Vasiljevic personally, but we understand your embarrassment, and we are very grateful for you having come. And as I say, you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, have you seen the filing by Mr. Domazet in relation to your expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I have not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it was filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have been finding it takes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And even I got mine this morning and I'm usually one of the last to get them. But Anyway, he takes the point, which is a valid one, that you have not complied with Rule 94 bis in that the documents must be filed 21 days before it is expected the witness will give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Dr. de Grave's report was filed on the 31st of August, so that would make this Thursday the earliest he could give evidence. Dr. Clark and Ms. Tabeau were filed on the 11th of September. Now, normally I would say to Mr. Domazet, "How long do you really need?" But I would be fearful of doing that unless it was by consent, because there was a decision last year, I think it was last year by the Appeals Chamber, which interpreted this group of rules permitting reports to be filed or written statements to be filed as if it was part of the American constitution, it I may say so, with all due respect to the Appeals Chamber, which had to be complied with strictly and there was no way in which you could apply Rule 127, for example, to extend or shorten the time. That indeed was the reason why Rule 92 bis, at the very end of it, has an express provision which says, "Unless otherwise ordered, something must be done in so many days." So may I suggest that you speak to Mr. Domazet or somebody from the Prosecution team, see if there can be some reshuffling of the witnesses so that Mr. Domazet does have sufficient time to consider them and to consult his experts. Dr. de Grave's evidence will be given only one day early, but if he's given one day early, and the Appeals Chamber follows its previous decision, we will all be in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have had some discussions with Mr. Domazet, if I could inform the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want to know what they are, but this is the very sort of thing that Mr. Domazet can consent to the witnesses being called earlier than 21 days from the filing. He in fact says he was only given the expertise of Dr. de Grave on the 11th of September, but I'm not sure how that could be so because it was filed on the 31st and those documents are faxed usually or put in the Defence box downstairs the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the things we have been discussing would require approval from the Court and that would be regarding Ms. Tabeau, and that would be to take her direct testimony this week and allow Mr. Domazet additional time before he conducts his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can't -- we can't consent to that because of this decision of the Appeals Chamber. It's -- it's a little unreal, if I may say so, in the present circumstances, because at the time that that decision was given, Rule 90 provided that subject to the Rules relating to depositions and videolink evidence, witnesses shall, in principle, be heard directly by the Chambers. Now, that has been repealed or deleted, and Rule 89(F) expresses it in a slightly more generous way. "A Chamber may receive the evidence of a witness orally or where the interests of justice allow in written form." That was to take away the preeminence, if I may put it that way, of oral evidence. But this is a very interesting issue, and one day it will have to be resolved, but I hope it's not going to be in this case as to whether that decision of the Appeals Chamber still applies in the light of that alteration of the Rules. It's not the sort of thing which, if I may say so, we should have to resolve in a case such as this where we can give you time to call these witnesses later. It's been suggested to me by those who know more than I do about what's going on in Trial Chamber II at the moment that we have an awful lot on our plates. My two colleagues here, fortunately don't have to worry about it but I certainly do, and if it means that you will not have enough witnesses to sit for example, this Friday, we need not sit on Friday because I am told that I will be kept busy all day doing other work, if that will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That will help us greatly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But my primary suggestion is that you and Mr. Domazet sort out how long he really needs, and hopefully Mr. Domazet, who seems to be very cooperative mostly, and properly looking after his client's interests, if he can say how long he really needs in order to prepare to deal with Ms. Tabeau and Dr. Clark, then you may get an agreement to call them earlier than the 21 days from the 11th of September, when their reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll speak with Mr. Domazet at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I think that will be a very good idea. Right. Well, next witness. Is VG59 your witness, Mr. Groome? Mr. Ossogo. I see. I'm sorry to have brought you down, Mr. Groome, but I thought this was a matter that was necessary to be resolved now so far as it can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for being absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I've said to you, you needn't be here all time. I was counsel for 20 years and I think I know just what is involved in preparation for a trial of this length. Yes, so now we've got Witness VG59. Yes, bring him in, would you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you make the solemn declaration in the form of the document which is being handed to you by the usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The pseudonym document will be Exhibit 76, P76, and it is under seal. Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness examine the information on this piece of paper containing his pseudonym as well as a certain number of particulars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you explained to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just going to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG59, the information contained on this piece of paper, don't, please, use the names of towns or the names of persons. You will simply give us the relationship you have with those persons as well as the letter of the alphabet. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Regarding the names of towns and villages, the letters of the alphabet. As for the relationship, you will simply tell us how you are related to a person, brother, sister, or whatever. And as regards one particular relationship, you will say VG104. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Sorry, VG64. 64, not 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm now a little lost, Mr. Ossogo. If he wishes to refer to the person who has that relationship to him, does he refer to him by the relationship or by the pseudonym or by the name? Obviously not the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. This applies to only one particular relative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But does he refer to her by the pseudonym VG64 or by the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have indicated here the relationship. So we have told him that he should use the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's probably too late now, but I would have suggested that they should have been in reverse order, with the relationship first and the pseudonym second, and then it would be consistent with all the others. As long as we all understand what it is he has to do, and more importantly, if the witness understands what he has to do. So if he wants to refer to the person who has that relationship in the second line, he refers to her by the pseudonym VG64 and does not refer to the relationship she has with him. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 59, for being at the disposal of the Chamber this morning to testify about the facts you experienced and which we will review in some detail. VG59, in 1989, were you a reserve police officer in the region that is indicated as region P?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What was this police unit in charge of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: It engaged in the training regarding weapons, and it got together once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was this unit subsequently mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: On the 24th of September, 1991, it was in active duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Have you done your obligatory military service in the 1970s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th of November, 1976, and I was discharged on the 18th of January, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And during your military service, did you learn how to handle weapons as well as how to identify various firearms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When did the members of the JNA enter your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: The Uzice Corps of the JNA entered at the end of April, and it left Visegrad on the 19th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After the Uzice Corps left, was there trouble in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: After the Uzice Corps had left, problems arose in my village. A group of Serbs appeared that called themselves the White Eagles. At least that is how they introduced themselves to us. One day - it was in the afternoon - a group of White Eagles arrived and people called -- of A1 were assembled in the house of VG64.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: This group of White Eagles, as you said, consisted of how many people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I noticed about ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you identify a particular person who could have been the leader of the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Not immediately, but I saw this Mitar Vasiljevic, who stood at the door of the house. He had a red ribbon on his left shoulder. He was armed with an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: To go back to the exact date, could you give us the month and possibly the date itself, if you can remember, and the year of course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but this was after the Uzice Corps had left. So it would be the end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: As you said a moment ago, you noticed the presence of Mitar Vasiljevic among this group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What was he doing in this group? What did they exactly do when they came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He played the part of a guard so that none of us would leave the house, and the other Eagles were looting the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He was wearing black trousers and some sort of black jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was he also wearing the red ribbon that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, on his left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, with an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to identify the type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: It was an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How were you able to identify it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Because I'm quite familiar with that weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did he speak to you or to anyone else at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He didn't speak to me, but he did speak to my brother. He asked him whether anyone was hiding in the attic, and he said that he would be the first to go up to the attic and let Mitar follow him to make sure that there was no one there. So Mitar believed him that there was no one in the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did he speak to your older brother or any other of your brothers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: To my older brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did they actually go to check whether anyone was hiding in the attic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No. Mitar believed what he heard, that there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was he aggressive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What did you feel seeing him armed with an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He told us that they were looking for a certain Avdo who had killed a Serb woman and two children and that they were searching the houses to arrest him, and I believed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you know Mitar Vasiljevic before you met on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Under which circumstances did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: We went to school together. Actually, he went to school with my brother. They were in the eighth grade and I was in the seventh grade. I knew him as a waiter too. I would often visit his bar where he worked, and he would serve at my table on innumerable occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: For how long were you together in the same school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: For four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where was this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: In B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you maintain good relations with him? Were you on good terms with him as neighbours or comrades or friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Could you explain the question for me, please? You said good neighbourly relations or schoolmates? What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: While you were at school together and possibly did you have any relationship outside school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: We were on very good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You said that he was a waiter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In which cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He worked in the Panos catering enterprise, which had several facilities. He worked in the hotel, in the Panos restaurant, in the Mezalin cafe also known as Cadza, and that is where I went to most often, because nearby, VG64 worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What did you do as a rule? Did you take coffee or a drink while he was working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: When I was not away on business, I would always go to his place waiting for him -- waiting for VG64 to complete her job, to come out of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you meet him only in this cafe or in other coffee shops or other places where he worked later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: We would often meet in the street. He always went to work on foot, and he would pass by my company, which was right on the road. So we would meet as he went to work, as we went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did he continue to work in the same place or was he assigned to other coffee shops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He worked for about half a year in the Cadza coffee shop and then he was moved to some other catering establish. I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's 11.00. We will adjourn now and resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG59, we shall resume our interrogation. We were speaking about your relationship with Mr. Vasiljevic, and you provided some information about him, indicating that you knew him. Now I'd like to go back to the first incident which you had to deal with. Can you be perhaps more specific and tell us in which house, in whose house you were found yourself, yourself and other people, and how many were there in that house when you were visited by the group of the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: We were in the house of my father. Well, between 25 and 30 people were confined there, including women and children and younger and older people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you exposed to -- all of you or some of you to harassment or any form of violence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I and all of us who were in that house, we were not mistreated by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After the group had left your village, did you note the disappearance of some of your personal property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. When I came home, I found VG64, who was crying, and I asked her what the matter was, and she said, "They found our money, and they took it away."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The other people that were with you, did they complain? Did they have similar grievances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. Many of them told me that money had disappeared and jewellery had disappear, but I don't know how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The day following that first incident, was there another group that visited you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Two days later, the same group returned, headed by Milan Lukic, who, during the first incident, had promised us that we should go back to our everyday business, and if we were to note some unknown persons, that we should report them to their patrols. In the second incident, they came, Milan and his people. They came in the afternoon hours when people were with their livestock in the pastures. Then they took away nine of my neighbours, either from the field or took them out of houses. And even today we have no information about those neighbours. There is no trace of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic, was he a member of the group that had visited you on that second occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: During the second incident, I did not see Mitar, but I assumed he was there because he belonged to that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of the nine men who were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Well, I can say -- I can tell you their names and surnames if the Court so allows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are any of these protected people?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Not as far as we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you go ahead and give us their names and surnames if you are able to do so, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Adil Vatres, and his brother-in-law Muhamed Hodzic, Uzeir Vila and his son Suljo Vila, Mustafa Vila and his son Nermin Vila, Kasim Murtic, Rasim Sehic and his son Enver Sehic, nicknamed Kender.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After having taken away these nine men, in what direction did the group move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: That group went in the direction of B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you note that some personal property, belongings were missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: On a different occasion, your brother and yourself, were you forced to go in a certain direction? Were you forced to move in a certain direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, but this occurred during the third incident when the whole local population of A1, A2, A3 were rounded up in the house of my neighbour. If it is necessary, I can quote his name and surname. One of the members of the White Eagles put a handkerchief on the floor and ordered us to take all the money and jewellery from our pockets and put it on that handkerchief. I was holding on to my daughter, and I took off her earrings and put it on that handkerchief. Afterwards, ten minutes later, a man of an average height, thin in the face, very pronounced black moustache, enter the house, and his nickname was Crnogorac. He ordered me and my brother to follow him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Well, we went in the direction of Vilina Vlas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What is Vilina Vlas? Is that a private home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: It is a hotel. Vilina Vlas is a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: When we came to the reception of the hotel, I saw a big black flag, and on it was a skull where it said, "We trust in God for King and Motherland." We were forced to kiss the flag three times and to cross ourselves three times. Then we were taken to the ground floor of the hotel. We passed through a corridor, and we were confined in a room which was about nine to ten square metres, where there were no windows. So it was difficult to breathe. In that room, I saw four of my neighbours from the neighbouring village who were tied with wire, with their hands behind their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG59, the flag, what sort of flag was that? Which country did it belong to? To which ethnic group? Can you give us some features of that flag as you had seen the flag upon entering the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Well, I never seen a flag like that in the whole world, and I suppose that it was a Chetnik flag with a skull on it so as to intimidate the population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Have you already heard or seen the words that were written on the flag and that were around this skull?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Around the head, the skull -- these were the words written around the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know the exact contents of those words or do you remember them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. I know what was written on the flag, but what the meaning for them was, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: It was said actually, "We trust in God, for King and Motherland"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Now to go back to the four people you found there and you knew therein in the Vilina Vlas Hotel, in the room without windows. Could you perhaps tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Bajro Murtic, Ibrahim Murtic, Bajro's son; Mehmed Menzilovic, Ismet Menzilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What happened subsequently in that room where you were confined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: In that room, we were closed in that room. We were confined there. And no one came to our door during the whole night. The room was so small for five, actually, six people, we sat throughout the night. In the morning when the doors were opened, I noticed that dawn had already broken, and two soldiers came. They were wearing on their heads caps called Sajkaca. One was blonde and had a big blonde beard. He swore at our Turkish mothers, although we are not Turks. He asked where Murat was, for whom we had voted. We told him that we did not know where Murat was. They told us, "You aren't speaking now, but you will speak on red coal," and then they went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Who is this Murat you voted for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No, I didn't vote for Murat. Murat is a person -- if you remember the incident regarding the electric power station and dam in Visegrad, he was the one who wanted to blow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which ethnic group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After having passed the night in the Hotel Vilina Vlas, were you visited the next day in your room, other than the visit of the two soldiers the day before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. Sredoje Lukic visited us, as well as Niko Vujicic, whom I knew very well. They were policemen -- they were policemen in Visegrad. They asked me who had brought me and why they had brought me. I simply answered I did not know. For that reason, that Milan Lukic was a close relative of Sredoje Lukic. They asked us if we had had breakfast, and we answered that they hadn't, and then they went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did they return subsequently, later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did come back. They came back in the afternoon, and they took me away. They took me to an office on the floor above to question me about who in village A had weapons, who had weapons in village A. I told him who had weapons there. They asked me who had fired at their patrol a few days before. I told them that I didn't know, because no one could have fired because the army had rounded up and disarmed the whole local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you spend some more time in the Hotel Vilina Vlas or were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: After that interview, I was returned there. I was returned to the hotel, in the room where we had been confined, but they told me before that that they would let me go. And I told them that my brother was also confined there, and they told me that they would release both me and my brother. About two hours later, Sredoje Lukic came again, and Niko Vujicic, too, and they told me, me and my brother, that we could go out and -- through the corridor and exit, that we could sit in a white Volkswagen whose previous owner was Himzo Demir, who was director of the secondary school centre. They, I must admit, took us home again. When we got home, we had a cup of coffee, and they told us, "Don't allow them to capture you again because we might not be able to help you in that case."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I spent another two days at home. So did my brother. After two days, at about 10.30 in the evening, we swam across the Drina River and reached the left bank of the Drina where it was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did the Office of the Prosecutor show you photographs so that you could identify the persons on the photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question. What do you mean when we spoke? You mean in the courtroom or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you were visited by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, did he show you photographs on which you recognised one person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: We're going to show them to you so that you can confirm whether this photo array was indeed the one shown to you at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, it is. These are the same photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which one did you recognise, the one you're pointing at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: As for the Chamber, perhaps it better to show it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does it contain a signature that would identify the witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I signed on the back side, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signature is on the back side, and it is Exhibit 55-VG59, which has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Has it? Not according to my records.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Would you please show the Chamber the person that you identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you look around the courtroom? Is he here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: In the last row over there, wearing a white shirt. You can just see his collar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, are you going to tender that document? It's not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. It is 55.VG13, VG13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is in evidence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you were describing what you yourself called the first incident which occurred towards the end of May when this group arrived in your village for the first time and when you saw, among others, Mitar Vasiljevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was a bit unclear in your answer when you were asked who led that group. Was that Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. While Mitar was standing at the doorway in the role of guard, after a certain amount of time, Milan Lukic appeared with a black hat on his head. He was armed with a light machine-gun, M52, and he told us that we were free to go back to our daily chores. One of our neighbours asked whether they could look after their livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please will you answer my questions, because I think what you're saying now is something that occurred later, when the whole village assembled. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No. This occurred during the first incident, in the first incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, during the first incident, but let me clear it up, if I can. You had this conversation at home first when the whole village was not assembled there. There were members of your family with Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic at the doorway. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And it was only later, at the request of Milan Lukic, one of your men, one of your people went to call the other locals and they got together in that house; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I don't know who went, but I personally, my wife and children, were brought to this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you arrive before the other locals to that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you arrived, who was already in the house, in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: My father, my brother, my sister-in-law, my brother's children, my stepmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And there was also Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic in the doorway. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic was in the doorway first, and then about ten minutes later, Milan Lukic arrived as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see them arriving in the village by car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic in the same car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you notice where they stopped, who got out of the car and who went in which direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: When I headed for my father's house, the car was parked just below my father's house, on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which car was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: It was a BMW. Then there was a Zastava 101 and a Zastava 128.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you saw those three vehicles parked, but were they already empty or were people inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No. There was no one inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And then you headed for your father's house, and you said that Mitar Vasiljevic was in the doorway; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But if I understood you correctly, Milan Lukic had still not arrived in the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see him prior to that or, rather, did you see him where he was if he was not in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I didn't see where he was until he enter the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could he have been searching the house, that same house, in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I assume he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic tell you that he was looking for this Avdo who had allegedly killed a Serb woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No. Mitar Vasiljevic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Regarding this incident, you already made a statement to the investigator prior to this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever mention this Avdo in those prior statements or that Mitar had said that that was the reason for their arrival in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you're claiming that in your statement to the investigators, you said that Mitar Vasiljevic had said that they were looking for an Avdo who had killed a Serb woman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What did Milan Lukic say in your presence before the other villagers arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Milan Lukic did not come before the other villagers arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that what you told the investigators in your earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said that Mitar Vasiljevic was on guard, guarding the house, was that your conclusion on the basis of the fact that he was in the doorway at the entrance to the house or did he tell you that he was the guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: He didn't say he was the guard, but if he was standing in the doorway, armed, then he could have been nothing other than a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I see. So you concluded that he was a guard because all the time he stood at the entrance to the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When the other villagers assembled later on, you mentioned a number, between 25 and 30, did Milan Lukic say anything then, and if he did so, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: When he arrived, he said that we should go back to our usual business. And as I mentioned, one of the neighbours said -- asked whether they could tend the livestock normally, and he said we could. And he said if we should note any unfamiliar people, that we should report it to his patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also said that that evening when this group left, that you personally, and the others who were living in other houses, were -- property was stolen from you. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Mitar Vasiljevic participate in that or could he have participated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No, because he was in the doorway all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were describing the second incident, you said that it occurred two days later and again it involved a Milan Lukic. Was there an incident the very next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did three soldiers come in a blue Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you describe that incident, which you failed to do a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Three men came in a blue Mercedes. One was an elderly man, maybe in his 50s, and two were much younger. One of them took my car, a Zastava 128, and he ordered me to go with him to the municipality building to authorise him to be able to use the car outside of Bosnia. I never saw my car again since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I see. So this was an incident that occurred the very next day after Milan Lukic's group first arrived in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That first incident, that is, the coming of Milan Lukic's group to your village, was that the first time you saw a group that called themselves the White Eagles in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Because you saw Mitar Vasiljevic with that group that evening, is that the reason why you assumed that he was a member of that group when you were answering questions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. So though in the second incident when these nine persons were taken away, whom you named, and though you didn't see Mitar Vasiljevic, you assumed that as he was part of the group two days before that incident, you assumed that he could have been in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Yes. Those are my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mentioned hearing Mitar Vasiljevic asking whether there was anyone in the attic and the answer that there was no one, was Milan Lukic present at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who was present then, all the persons that you listed a moment ago except Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: Could you explain that a little, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember who exactly was present at the time, members of your family, to avoid repeating all the names that you mentioned a moment ago as being present in that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG59
utterances.text: I was present and those I listed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
